Capturing the containment relations -- which clusters lie within other clusters ::: ::: :::: :::: {.fragment} These observations motivate the notion of __hierarchical__ clustering. In hierarchical clustering, we move away from the __partition__ notion of $k$-means, and instead capture a more complex arrangement that includes containment of one cluster within another. > Note: GMMs relax the partitioning notion further! :::: # Hierarchical Clustering Example ## Hierarchical Clustering Example Inspired by [Hastie & Tibshirani lecture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yktzn-Mr2Nw). :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {#ee1fafec .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=506 height=523} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"}

* We combine all points into a single cluster ::: :::: ## Example: Dendrogram ::: {#d9e831b7 .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-14-output-1.png){width=1142 height=567} ::: ::: ## Example: Dendrogram Explained ::: {#fd1e8087 .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-15-output-1.png){width=595 height=279 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} * In the dendrogram, the vertical axis is the distance between the clusters * The horizontal axis is the points * The clusters are merged from the bottom up ::: ## Example: Dendrogram cont. ::: {#2ec29688 .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-16-output-1.png){width=566 height=279 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: * We can now split the dendrogram at a certain level to get a clustering # Hierarchical Clustering A hierarchical clustering produces a set of __nested__ clusters organized into a tree. A hierarchical clustering is visualized using a __dendrogram__ * A tree-like diagram that records the containment relations among clusters. ![](./figs/L08-dendrogram.png){width="600px" fig-align="center"} ## Strengths of Hierarchical Clustering ![](./figs/L08-dendrogram.png){width="400px" fig-align="center"} Hierarchical clustering has a number of advantages: :::: {.incremental} * Encodes many __different__ clusterings. * It does not itself decide on the correct number of clusters. * A clustering is obtained by "cutting" the dendrogram at some level. * You can make this crucial decision yourself, by inspecting the dendrogram. * You can obtain a (somewhat) arbitrary number of clusters. :::: ## Another advantage Another advantage is that the dendrogram may itself correspond to a meaningful structure, for example, a taxonomy. ![](./figs/L08-animal-taxonomy.jpg){height="100%" fig-align="center"} ## Yet another advantage * Many hierarchical clustering methods can be performed using either similarity (proximity) or dissimilarity (distance) metrics. * This can be very helpful! * Techniques like $k$-means rely on a specific way of measuring similarity or distance between data points. ## Compared to $k$-means Another aspect of hierachical clustering is that it can handle certain cases better than $k$-means. Because of the nature of the $k$-means algorithm, $k$-means tends to produce: * Roughly spherical clusters * Clusters of approximately equal size * Non-overlapping clusters In many real-world situations, clusters may not be round, they may be of unequal size, and they may overlap. Hence we would like clustering algorithms that can work in those cases also. ## In-Class Exercise Create a hierarchical cluster and dendogram for this data. ::: {#52ed2b2a .cell execution_count=16} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-17-output-1.png){width=950 height=470 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: # Hierarchical Clustering Algorithms ## Hierarchical Clustering Algorithms There are two main approaches to hierarchical clustering: "bottom-up" and "top-down." ::: {.fragment} __Agglomerative__ Clustering ("bottom-up"): * Start by defining each point as its own cluster * At each successive step, merge the two clusters that are closest to each other * Repeat until only one cluster is left. ::: ::: {.fragment} __Divisive__ Clustering ("top-down"): * Start with one, all-inclusive cluster * At each step, find the cluster split that creates the largest distance between resulting clusters * Repeat until each point is in its own cluster. ::: ## Some key points * Agglomerative techniques are by far the more common. * The key to both of these methods is defining __the distance between two clusters.__ * Different definitions for the inter-cluster distance yield different clusterings. ::: {.fragment} To illustrate the impact of the choice of cluster distances, we'll focus on agglomerative clustering. ::: ## Hierarchical Clustering Algorithm Inputs 1. __Input data__ as either * __2-D sample/feature matrix__ * __1D condensed distance matrix__ -- upper triangular of pairwise distance matrix flattened 2. The cluster __linkage__ method (__single__, complete, average, ward, ...) 3. The __distance metric__ (_Euclidean_, manhattan, Jaccard, ...) ## Hierarchical Clustering Algorithm Output An $(n-1,4)$ shaped __linkage matrix__. Where __each row__ is `[idx1, idx2, dist, sample_count]` is a single step in the clustering process and `idx1` and `idx2` are indices of the cluster being merged, where * indices $\{ 0...n-1 \}$ refer to the original data points and * indices $\{n, n+1, ...\}$ refer to each new cluster created And `sample_count` is the number of original data samples in the new cluster. ## Linkage Matrix Example Let's calculate and display the linkage matrix for our 5 data points A-E: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {#f81b704a .cell execution_count=17} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linkage Matrix for 5 data points A-E: Format: [idx1, idx2, distance, sample_count] ================================================== [[0. 2. 1.13137085 2. ] [3. 4. 1.41421356 2. ] [1. 5. 2.05588586 3. ] [6. 7. 5.66085977 5. ]] ================================================== Interpretation: Row 0: Merge points 0 and 2 (A and C) at distance 1.13 Row 1: Merge points 3 and 4 (D and E) at distance 1.41 Row 2: Merge point 1 (B) with cluster 5 (A&C) at distance 2.06 Row 3: Merge cluster 6 (A&B&C) with cluster 7 (D&E) at distance 5.66 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](./figs/L08-dendrogram.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} ::: :::: ## Hierarchical Clustering Algorithm Explained 1. __Initialization__ * Start with each data point as its own cluster. * Calculate the distance matrix if not provided 2. __Iterative Clustering__ * At each step, the two closest clusters (according to linkage method and distance metric) are merged into a new cluster. * The distance between new cluster and the remaining clusters is added * Repeat previous two steps until only one cluster remains. ## Defining Cluster Proximity Given two clusters, how do we define the _distance_ between them? Here are three natural ways to do it. ## Cluster Proximity -- Single-Linkage ![](./figs/L08-hierarchical-criteria-a.jpeg){height="300px" fig-align="center"} __Single-Linkage:__ the distance between two clusters is the distance between the closest two points that are in different clusters. $$ D_\text{single}(i,j) = \min_{x, y}\{d(x, y) \,|\, x \in C_i, y \in C_j\} $$ ## Cluster Proximity -- Complete-Linkage ![](./figs/L08-hierarchical-criteria-b.jpeg){height="300px" fig-align="center"} __Complete-Linkage:__ the distance between two clusters is the distance between the farthest two points that are in different clusters. $$ D_\text{complete}(i,j) = \max_{x, y}\{d(x, y) \,|\, x \in C_i, y \in C_j\} $$ ## Cluster Proximity -- Average-Linkage ![](./figs/L08-hierarchical-criteria-c.jpeg){height="300px" fig-align="center"} __Average-Linkage:__ the distance between two clusters is the average distance between all pairs of points from different clusters. $$ D_\text{average}(i,j) = \frac{1}{|C_i|\cdot|C_j|}\sum_{x \in C_i,\, y \in C_j}d(x, y) $$ ## Cluster Proximity Example Notice that it is easy to express the definitions above in terms of similarity instead of distance. Here is a set of 6 points that we will cluster to show differences between distance metrics. ::: {#92c90738 .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-19-output-1.png){width=466 height=315 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Cluster Proximity Example, cont. ::: We can calculate the distance matrix ::: {#aad0a643 .cell execution_count=19} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}

p0 0.00 0.23 0.22 0.37 0.34 0.24
p1 0.23 0.00 0.14 0.19 0.14 0.24
p2 0.22 0.14 0.00 0.16 0.28 0.10
p3 0.37 0.19 0.16 0.00 0.28 0.22
p4 0.34 0.14 0.28 0.28 0.00 0.39
p5 0.24 0.24 0.10 0.22 0.39 0.00
``` ::: ::: ## Single-Linkage Clustering :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](./figs/L08-singlelink-pointset.png){width="600px"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {#03dfe20d .cell execution_count=20} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-21-output-1.png){width=802 height=414} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Single Linkage Clustering Advantages Single-linkage clustering can handle non-elliptical shapes. Here we use SciPy's [fcluster](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.cluster.hierarchy.fcluster.html) to form flat custers from hierarchical clustering. ::: {#0e200a98 .cell execution_count=21} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-22-output-1.png){width=763 height=389 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Single Linkage Advantages, cont. ::: Single-Linkage can find different sized clusters: ::: {#662b2851 .cell execution_count=22} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-23-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: ## Single Linkage Disadvantages Single-linkage clustering can be sensitive to noise and outliers. The results can change drastically on even slightly more noisy data. ::: {#63a3ebcf .cell execution_count=23} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-24-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"} ## Single Linkage Disadvantages, cont. ::: And here's another example where we bump the standard deviation on the clusters slightly. ::: {#12b92621 .cell execution_count=24} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-25-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: ## Complete-Linkage Clustering :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](./figs/L08-completelink-pointset.png){width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {#224fceb6 .cell execution_count=25} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-26-output-1.png){width=802 height=414} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Complete-Linkage Clustering Advantages Produces more-balanced clusters -- more-equal diameters ::: {#ba814fc9 .cell execution_count=26} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-27-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: ::: {#8916b471 .cell execution_count=27} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-28-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: Less susceptible to noise: ::: {#29953fd4 .cell execution_count=28} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-29-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: ## Complete-Linkage Clustering Disadvantages Some disadvantages for complete-linkage clustering are: - Sensitivity to outliers - Tendency to compute more compact, spherical clusters - Computationally intensive for large datasets. ## Average-Linkage Clustering :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](./figs/L08-averagelink-pointset.png){width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {#eadff356 .cell execution_count=29} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-30-output-1.png){width=802 height=414} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Average-Linkage Clustering Strengths and Limitations Average-Linkage clustering is in some sense a compromise between Single-linkage and Complete-linkage clustering. __Strengths:__ * Less susceptible to noise and outliers __Limitations:__ * Biased toward elliptical clusters ## Average-Linkage Clustering Strengths and Limitations, cont. Produces more isotropic clusters. ::: {#5e762499 .cell execution_count=30} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-31-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: ## Average-Linkage Clustering Strengths and Limitations, cont. More resistant to noise than Single-Linkage. ::: {#d4c92eb3 .cell execution_count=31} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-32-output-1.png){width=763 height=389} ::: ::: ## All Three Compared ::: {layout-ncol="3"} ![Single-Linkage](./figs/L08-singlelink-pointset.png){width="100%"} ![Complete-Linkage](./figs/L08-completelink-pointset.png){width="100%"} ![Average-Linkage](./figs/L08-averagelink-pointset.png){width="100%"} ::: ## Ward's Distance Finally, we consider one more cluster distance. Ward's distance asks "What if we combined these two clusters -- how would clustering improve?" To define "how would clustering improve?" we appeal to the $k$-means criterion. So: __Ward's Distance__ between clusters $C_i$ and $C_j$ is the difference between the total within cluster sum of squares for the two clusters separately, __compared to__ the _within cluster sum of squares_ resulting from merging the two clusters into a new cluster $C_{i+j}$: $$ D_\text{Ward}(i, j) = \sum_{x \in C_i} (x - c_i)^2 + \sum_{x \in C_j} (x - c_j)^2 - \sum_{x \in C_{i+j}} (x - c_{i+j})^2 $$ where $c_i, c_j, c_{i+j}$ are the corresponding cluster centroids. ## Ward's Distance continued In a sense, this cluster distance results in a hierarchical analog of $k$-means. As a result, it has properties similar to $k$-means: * Less susceptible to noise and outliers * Biased toward elliptical clusters Hence it tends to behave more like average-linkage hierarchical clustering. # Hierarchical Clustering in Practice ## In Practice Now we'll look at doing hierarchical clustering in practice. We'll use 1/10th of the synthetic data set from the beginning of this lecture. [scipy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/index.html) has a comprehensive set of [clustering tools](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/cluster.hierarchy.html). ::: {#476b57f1 .cell execution_count=32} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](08-Clustering-III-hierarchical_files/figure-revealjs/cell-33-output-1.png){width=389 height=389 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ## In Practice, cont. Top terms per cluster when we flatten to a depth of 5. ::: {#cabc42d8 .cell execution_count=40} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cluster 1: space nasa edu henry gov alaska access com moon digex Cluster 2: ax max b8f g9v a86 145 1d9 pl 2di 0t Cluster 3: edu com year baseball article writes cs team game university Cluster 4: risc instruction ghhwang csie set nctu cisc tw reduced mq Cluster 5: windows edu file dos com files card drivers driver use ``` ::: ::: ## Comparison of Linkages Scikit-Learn has a very nice [notebook](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/cluster/plot_linkage_comparison.html) and plot, copied here, that shows the different clusters resulting from different linkage methods. ![](./figs/L08-sphx_glr_plot_linkage_comparison_001.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"} # Recap ## Clustering Recap This wraps up our _partitional_ Cluster topics. We covered: ::: {.incremental} * What the clustering problem is * An overview of the $k$-means clustering algorithm including initialization with $k$-means++ * Visualization techniques such as Multi-Dimensional Scaling * Cluster evaluation with (Adjusted) Rand Index and Silhouette Coefficient * Using evaluation to determine number of clusters * Hierarchical Clustering with different methods and metrics * Looked at applications of clustering on various types of synthetic data, image color quantization, newsgroup clustering :::
